Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $T>0$, $0<\epsilon<T$, an integer $d\ge1$, and an integer $N\ge1$. Let $X_t\in\mathbb R^d$ be a continuous nonexplosive Markov diffusion on $[\epsilon,T]$, where nonexplosive means its paths remain in $\mathbb R^d$ on the whole interval, and Markov means its conditional future law given the past depends only on its current state. Write $P_t(A)=P(X_t\in A)$ for its law on each Borel set $A$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $W$ be an adapted standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are independent of the earlier filtration and have laws $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$. Let $b_t(x)\in\mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma_t(x)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be Borel maps. The process is a continuous Brownian Itô process in the sense that, up to indistinguishability,

$$X_t=X_\epsilon+\int_\epsilon^t b_r(X_r)\,dr+\left(\sum_{j=1}^d\int_\epsilon^t\sigma_{ij}(r,X_r)\,dW_r^j\right)_{i=1}^d,$$

where the drift integrals are pathwise Lebesgue integrals and the coordinate stochastic integrals are localized Itô integrals; assume $\int_\epsilon^T|b_r(X_r)|\,dr<\infty$ and $\int_\epsilon^T\|\sigma_r(X_r)\|_F^2\,dr<\infty$ almost surely, with $\|M\|_F^2=\sum_{i,j}|M_{ij}|^2$. Assume also that $\sigma_t(x)$ is invertible with $\sup_{t,x}\|\sigma_t(x)^{-1}\|<\infty$. Put $a_t(x)=\sigma_t(x)\sigma_t(x)^{\mathsf T}$. A transition density $q(s,x;t,y)$ means that $P(X_t\in dy\mid X_s=x)=q(s,x;t,y)\,dy$.

Assume the marginal densities $p_t$ and transition densities $q(s,x;t,y)$ are positive, finite, and normalized with respect to Lebesgue measure; $p_t$ has one continuous time derivative and two continuous state derivatives. For $\epsilon\le s<t\le T$, assume

$$p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)\,dx,\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz\quad(s<r<t).$$

For $L_t\phi=b_t\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}a_{t,ij}\partial_i\partial_j\phi$, define $L_t^*r=-\sum_i\partial_i(b_{t,i}r)+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}r)$. Assume $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ and $\partial_tq(s,x;t,y)=L_t^{*,y}q(s,x;t,y)$ classically. For every compactly supported smooth test, assume transition integrals and their time derivatives are absolutely integrable, differentiation under those integrals is valid, and integration by parts in space has no boundary term.

For $0\le u<T-\epsilon$, set $s=T-u$ and define the reverse score $s_s(x)=\nabla_x\log p_s(x)$. With $a=\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T}$ and $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$, define the reverse drift supplied by the positive-density reversal interface:

$$\widetilde b_u(x)=-b_{T-u}(x)+(\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u})(x)+a_{T-u}(x)s_{T-u}(x),\qquad \widetilde\sigma_u(x)=\sigma_{T-u}(x).$$

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ for infinitely differentiable real functions with compact support. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define $\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}a_{T-u,ij}\partial_i\partial_j\phi$. Assume that for every reverse initial law the martingale problem for $\widetilde L_u$ has a unique nonexplosive continuous solution in law; this means that each compact-test compensated process $\phi(Y_u)-\phi(Y_0)-\int_0^u\widetilde L_r\phi(Y_r)\,dr$ is a local martingale and its law is unique. The current reversal supplier's proof uses AC through its Brownian-reconstruction lemma, so AC is an explicit algorithm assumption here.

Set $S=T-\epsilon$, $h=S/N$, $u_k=kh$, and $t_k=T-u_k$ for $0\le k\le N$. Given step sizes $\eta_k>0$, the **predictor-corrector score-sampling algorithm** takes an initial draw $Y_0\sim P_T$ and mutually independent vectors $G_k,\xi_k\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, independent of $Y_0$. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, perform the following two operations:

1. **Predictor.** Compute one Euler–Maruyama step for the reverse equation:
   $$\widehat Y_{k+1}=Y_k+h\widetilde b_{u_k}(Y_k)+\sqrt h\,\widetilde\sigma_{u_k}(Y_k)G_k.$$

2. **Corrector.** Let $U_{k+1}(x)=-\log p_{t_{k+1}}(x)$, so $e^{-U_{k+1}}$ is the normalized target density $p_{t_{k+1}}$. Apply one unadjusted Langevin update with step size $\eta_k$:
   $$Y_{k+1}=\widehat Y_{k+1}-\eta_k\nabla U_{k+1}(\widehat Y_{k+1})+\sqrt{2\eta_k}\,\xi_k=\widehat Y_{k+1}+\eta_k s_{t_{k+1}}(\widehat Y_{k+1})+\sqrt{2\eta_k}\,\xi_k.$$

Return $Y_N$, the finite-step state at forward time $\epsilon$. The procedure requires an exact marginal score on $[\epsilon,T]$ and starts from the actual terminal law $P_T$; it does not replace $P_T$ by $N_d(0,I_d)$ unless they are equal.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space, fix $x_0\in X$, and let $D<\infty$ satisfy $d(x,y)\le D$ for all $x,y\in X$. Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$, let $(Z,\Sigma,\rho)$ be a probability space, and let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open with $p\ge1$. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, let $G_\theta:Z\to X$ be measurable and define its law by $P_\theta(B)=\rho(G_\theta^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq X$. Assume $z\mapsto d(G_\theta(z),G_{\theta'}(z))$ is $\rho$-measurable for every $\theta,\theta'\in\Theta$, and that there is a measurable set $Z_0\subseteq Z$ with $\rho(Z_0)=1$ on which $\theta\mapsto G_\theta(z)$ is continuous. Let $\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$ be the class of bounded Borel functions $f:X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x_0)=0$ and $|f(x)-f(y)|\le d(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$, and set $V(\theta)=d_{\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)}(\mu,P_\theta)$. Then $V(\theta)=W_1^X(\mu,P_\theta)$ and $V$ is continuous on $\Theta$.

Suppose in addition that for every $\theta_0\in\Theta$ there are an open neighborhood $U\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$, a measurable $K_{\theta_0}:Z\to[0,+\infty)$ with $\int K_{\theta_0}\,d\rho<\infty$, and a measurable full-measure set $Z_{\theta_0}\subseteq Z$ such that, for every $z\in Z_{\theta_0}$ and every $\theta,\theta'\in U$,
$$
d(G_\theta(z),G_{\theta'}(z))\le K_{\theta_0}(z)\|\theta-\theta'\|.
$$
Then $V$ is locally Lipschitz, with $|V(\theta)-V(\theta')|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|\int K_{\theta_0}\,d\rho$ for $\theta,\theta'\in U$. At any such $\theta_0$ where $V$ is Fréchet differentiable, if the signed dual supremum at $\theta_0$ is attained by $f_{\theta_0}\in\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$ and $H_{\theta_0}(\theta,z)=f_{\theta_0}(G_\theta(z))$ is Fréchet differentiable in $\theta$ at $\theta_0$ for $\rho$-almost every $z$ with measurable derivative, then
$$
\nabla V(\theta_0)=-\int_Z\nabla_\theta H_{\theta_0}(\theta_0,z)\,d\rho(z).
$$
Here Fréchet differentiability of a scalar function $F$ at $\theta_0$ means there is a linear map $A$ such that $F(\theta_0+h)=F(\theta_0)+A[h]+o(\|h\|)$ as $h\to0$. The attainment and composite-differentiability assumptions are pointwise hypotheses for the gradient formula; compact dual attainment is not asserted.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

Assume AC. Fix a finite list $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Let $s$ be any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$, meaning that it agrees with the ordinary derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set; such a representative exists and is bounded by the Lipschitz constant. For every tuple of positive integer hidden widths $(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, use the width-normalized network with independent standard-normal initialization and scalar linear output.

Put

$$\Sigma^1_{ij}=\frac{x_i\cdot x_j}{n_0}+\beta^2.$$

For $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U_i,U_j)$ have the centered Gaussian law with variances $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii},\Sigma^{r-1}_{jj}$ and covariance $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ij}$, and define

$$\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad \dot\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[s(U_i)s(U_j)].$$

These Gaussian laws may be singular; their marginal variances are at least $\beta^2$, and their laws and expectations depend only on the displayed covariance. Define $\Theta^1_{ij}=\Sigma^1_{ij}$ and, for $r=2,\ldots,L$,

$$\Theta^r_{ij}=\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Sigma^r_{ij},\qquad K_\infty=(\Theta^L_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N.$$

At initialization, the finite-data neural tangent Gram matrix $K_0$ converges in probability to $K_\infty$ under the sequential hidden-width limit $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}$.

For the training conclusion, fix a horizon $T\ge0$. In addition, assume that $\sigma$ is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second derivative, that $d:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^N$ is measurable and integrable, and that for each width tuple a differentiable parameter path $\theta(t)$ exists on $[0,T]$ and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)d_i(t).$$

Write $f_t(x)=f_{\theta(t)}(x)$ and $K_t(i,j)=K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j)$, where $K_\theta$ is the finite-network neural tangent kernel. Define $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential limit, meaning that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ makes the iterated-limit upper bound on $\mathbb P(\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt>M)$ less than $\varepsilon$. Then

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$

where $\|\cdot\|_{op}$ is the Euclidean operator norm. Along the path,

$$\dot f_t(x_i)=-\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K_t(i,j)d_j(t),$$

and

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\|f_t-f_0+\frac1N\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\right\|_N\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability}.$$

Thus the finite-time output equation has the deterministic limiting kernel as its generator in the precise integrated-error sense displayed above.
